name: Stinging nettle (Urtica dioica)
short: Case reports: hives all over a 17-day-old whose mother put nettle water on her nipples; breast discharge on a nettle supplement. Touch: itching, dermatitis, hives. Trials in men: few side effects.
text: Skin contact with the hairs on the stems and leaves of the stinging nettle plant releases chemicals that cause itching, dermatitis and urticaria (hives) within moments, according to a review. Trials in men with benign prostatic hyperplasia reported few side effects: a 6-month randomized placebo-controlled trial of Urtica dioica in 620 men identified no side effects in either group (the abstract does not name the plant part or route), and a 12-month randomized placebo-controlled trial of a dry nettle root extract in 246 men reported fewer adverse events with the extract than with placebo (29 vs 38); a review of nettle root judged the risk of adverse events and toxicity very low but said pre-clinical safety data remain to be completed. Case reports describe new-onset galactorrhoea (milky breast discharge) in a 30-year-old woman who had been taking a 500 mg stinging nettle supplement for a month for allergies (the abstract does not state the route; she also used Echinacea intermittently and had an etonogestrel implant), which resolved one week after the nettle alone was stopped, and generalised urticaria in a 17-day-old breastfed infant whose mother had applied water boiled with stinging nettle to her nipples, which had cleared completely without treatment by the second day in hospital. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
